title: How to Think: Candidate Moves and the Move-Selection Routine

exercises.question: Black to move. In the Two Knights Defence (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5), taking back on d5 with the knight looks completely natural. Run your blunder check first, then play the best move.
exercises.explanation: Before recapturing, ask what White's forcing replies would be. After 5...Nxd5? White has 6.Nxf7! Kxf7 7.Qf3+, the Fried Liver Attack: your king is dragged into the open and the pinned knight on d5 is attacked again. 5...Na5! instead hits the bishop on c4, and after 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 Black gets quick development for the pawn. 5...b5 and 5...Nd4 are sharp alternatives that also avoid the trap.

wrong.why: 6.Nxf7! Kxf7 7.Qf3+ — the Fried Liver Attack, and your king is in great danger.
It attacks the queen, but 6.Nxf7 forks your queen and rook first.

exercises.hint: If you take on d5, which white sacrifice on f7 becomes possible?
exercises.objective: Check the opponent's forcing replies before making a 'natural' recapture.

exercises.question: Black to move. Your rook has reached the second rank, and both b2 and f2 look tempting. First ask what White is threatening, then play the best move.
exercises.explanation: Step one of the routine is 'what does my opponent want?' Your back rank has no defender: the queen on b6 and the rook on c2 are far away, and your king has no flight square, so White threatens Re8#. That is why 25...Qxb2?? and 25...Rxb2?? both lose at once to 26.Re8#. 25...g6 (or 25...h6) gives the king an escape square; after that White has no threat, and the pressure on b2 and f2 is still yours.

wrong.why: 26.Re8# — the free pawn does not count if you are mated.
26.Re8# — nothing can block or capture on the back rank.

exercises.objective: Start every move by asking what the opponent threatens, even when you have tempting captures.

exercises.question: White to move. Black has just played 7...Ng4. Count the attackers and defenders of f2, then choose the best move.
exercises.explanation: f2 is attacked twice (Bc5 and Ng4) and defended only by the king. Castling adds the f1-rook as a defender and takes the king off the e1-a5 diagonal and the e-file, so ...Bxf2+ is no longer a threat; White can follow with h3 to kick the knight. 8.Qe2? also guards f2, but 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 still wins a pawn and leaves the king stuck in the middle.

wrong.why: 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 — the pawn falls anyway and your king can no longer castle.
Opening the centre while f2 is under fire only helps Black's pieces; after 8...exd4 the weaknesses multiply.

exercises.hint: Which move adds a defender to f2 and improves the king at the same time?
exercises.objective: Count attackers and defenders of a target square before choosing a defence.

exercises.question: White to move. In the Scotch (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 Qe7 7.Qe2 Nd5 8.c4) Black has played 8...Ba6, and the knight on d5 is attacked by your c-pawn. Your first idea is 9.cxd5. Compare it with at least one other candidate and play the best move.
exercises.explanation: The 'free' knight is a trap. The bishop on a6 is aimed at your queen on e2, and only the c4-pawn stands between them, so the pawn is pinned. If it captures, 9.cxd5? Bxe2 10.Bxe2 Qxe5, Black has won the queen for a knight. The main line is 9.b3, defending c4 so that Black's knight has to move and the pin causes no harm; 9.Nd2 and 9.Qe4 are also fine. Your first idea is only a candidate until you have checked the opponent's best reply.

wrong.why: The c4-pawn was pinned to your queen: 9...Bxe2 wins the queen for a knight.

exercises.hint: What stands behind the c4-pawn on the diagonal from a6?
exercises.objective: Compare candidates by looking at the opponent's best reply, not your hoped-for one.

exercises.question: Black to move. The pawn on a2 is loose. Is it safe to take? Play the right move.
exercises.explanation: White's doubled rooks threaten Rd8+! Rxd8 Rxd8+ Ne8 Rxe8#. That threat exists already, so ...Qxa2 is not a candidate at all. Give the king an escape square with 20...h6 (or ...g6/...h5); then Black's extra piece will tell.

wrong.why: 21.Rd8+! Rxd8 22.Rxd8+ Ne8 23.Rxe8# — your queen is on a2 and cannot help.

exercises.hint: What are White's checks? Look at d8.
exercises.objective: Spot an opponent's threat that already exists before grabbing material.

exercises.question: White to move. Ne7+ wins Black's queen. When you see a good move, look for a better one.
exercises.explanation: The fork is good; checkmate is better. The queen on h5 and the bishop on d3 both hit h7, the f6-square is empty so no knight defends, and the black king's escape squares f8 and h8 are blocked or covered. Always finish the candidate list — checks first — before you play the first strong move you see.

wrong.why: It wins the queen, but Qxh7# ends the game at once.

exercises.hint: List every check, not just the first one you notice.
exercises.objective: Keep looking after finding a good move; checks that mate beat checks that win material.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's last move was 4.Nb5. What is the threat, and what is the best way to stop it?
exercises.explanation: Knight on b5 plus bishop on f4 both hit c7: White threatens Nxc7+ forking king and rook. 4...Na6 guards c7 with a developing move. 4...Bd6 (challenging the bishop) and 4...Bb4+ also work. The routine 4...Be7?, played on autopilot, loses material after 5.Nxc7+.

wrong.why: 5.Nxc7+ forks king and rook — a normal developing move that ignores the threat.
Hitting the bishop does not cover c7, and 5.dxe5 leaves Black a pawn down with problems.

exercises.hint: Which square do the knight and bishop both attack?
exercises.objective: Name the opponent's threat before choosing a developing move.

exercises.question: White to move. In the Open Ruy Lopez Black played 11...Qd7?, and after 12.Nxe6 fxe6 the knight on e4 looks safely protected by the d5-pawn. The natural move is 13.f3, kicking it. Compare candidates and play the best move.
exercises.explanation: Ask what the d5-pawn is doing. It guards the knight on e4, but it also blocks the d-file between your queen and Black's unprotected queen on d7. 13.Rxe4! exploits this double duty: if 13...dxe4, the d-file opens and 14.Qxd7 wins the queen; if Black does not take back, White has simply won a knight. The automatic 13.f3? allows 13...Bc5+ with active play for Black. This is the Tarrasch Trap: before playing the obvious move, check the captures.

wrong.why: 13...Bc5+ and Black's pieces come to life; the chance to win material is gone.
Natural development, but 13...Nxe5 wins a pawn for Black.

exercises.hint: Which black pawn has two jobs at once?
exercises.objective: Treat the obvious move as one candidate among several: first check captures that overload a defender.

exercises.question: Black to move. Your knight on d5 is attacked. List the candidate squares and play the best move.
exercises.explanation: A knight retreat is not the only candidate: 8...Ba6 pins the c4-pawn to the queen on e2, so the knight is safe for now and Black develops with tempo. 8...Nb6 is the solid retreat. 8...Nb4? and 8...Nf4? look active, but the knight lands on a square where it can be harassed and has no future.

wrong.why: After 9.a3 the knight must go back to a6, a passive square, and Black has lost time.
9.Qe4 (or 9.Qe3) attacks the knight, which has no safe retreat, and Black loses material.

exercises.hint: Can you make the attacking pawn unable to capture?
exercises.objective: Include counter-attacking and pinning moves in the candidate list, not just retreats.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's pawn attacks your knight on f6. One move keeps the game balanced — find it.
exercises.explanation: The natural candidates are knight moves (...Ne4, ...Ng4), but a counter-strike belongs on the list too. 6...d5! attacks the bishop on c4 and opens the c8-bishop; after 7.Bb5 Ne4 Black's knight sits on a strong central square. 6...Ne4? runs into 7.Bd5! and 6...Ng4 into 7.cxd4, both with the knight in trouble.

wrong.why: 7.Bd5! attacks the knight a second time and Black's position falls apart.
7.cxd4 leaves the knight offside and the bishop on c5 under attack; White is clearly better.

exercises.hint: Is there a move that creates a bigger threat than White's?
exercises.objective: Add counter-attacking pawn breaks to the candidate list when a piece is attacked.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's last move, 9...Ng4, attacks f2 for the second time. Your rook has left f1. Choose the best defence.
exercises.explanation: f2 is attacked by Ba7 and Ng4 and defended only by the king. 10.Re2 defends it calmly (10.Rf1, admitting the rook was misplaced, also works). The attacking-looking 10.h3? fails to 10...Nxf2, and 10.Qe2? to 10...Bxf2+ winning the exchange. Under pressure, compare the quiet defensive candidates; the flashy one often loses.

wrong.why: 10...Nxf2! — the knight takes on f2 instead of retreating and Black wins material.

exercises.hint: Count: two attackers on f2. How many defenders does your move add?
exercises.objective: Prefer a quiet defence that keeps the count in your favour over a 'tempo' move that does not.
